01

Machine learning
Language & evaluation

Mood Atlas

Exploring everyday emotions in text, with room for uncertainty.

A text-emotion demo that grew out of a team research project. The current version moves beyond three restrictive categories to a multilabel model that can also say when the signal is unclear.

My work: NLP preprocessing and model development in the original team project; the current repository documents the revised emotion baseline and its evaluation.

  • Python
  • scikit-learn
  • GoEmotions
  • Flask
Open demo ↗Source code
The problem, approach & results

The problem

The original classifier forced every sentence into depression, suicide, or non-suicide. That made ordinary statements a poor fit. The revised task is to identify expressed everyday emotions, allowing more than one label or no clear prediction.

Data & approach

The baseline uses Google’s GoEmotions dataset: 27 emotions plus neutral. After normalized exact deduplication, the official splits contain 43,189 training, 5,375 validation, and 5,379 test examples. Training-only TF-IDF features feed one-vs-rest logistic regression. Each label has a threshold selected on validation data; labels without a qualifying threshold abstain.

Evaluation

The repository reports these results on the untouched test split. They describe the learned model, not the separate tiredness phrase cue or the interface’s neutral-suppression policy.

Micro precision
0.673
Micro recall
0.389
Micro F1
0.493

At least one label is emitted on 62.4% of test examples. This makes the trade-off visible: the model leaves some text unanswered and misses some emotions. Inspect the evaluation record.

What I would improve next

Build a separately annotated set of everyday prompts, including neutral descriptions, mixed emotions, negation, and sarcasm. Compare a contextual encoder against this baseline on that same set. The old and new systems solve different tasks, so their scores are not a direct improvement comparison.

This demo classifies language. It does not diagnose mental-health conditions or assess someone’s actual state of mind.

02

Generative AI
Personalized images

Personalized Avatar Studio

One familiar face, imagined in different scenes.

A portrait-generation application using a personalized diffusion checkpoint. It explores the balance between keeping a recognizable subject and following a new scene description.

My project: a personalized avatar application, with a hosted studio and an explanation of its generation workflow.

  • Stable Diffusion
  • Diffusers
  • PyTorch
  • Gradio
Explore the studio ↗Source code
The idea, model & limitations

The idea

Use a personalized image model to place the same subject in different settings. The app adds an identity cue to a scene prompt, then generates a portrait from a selectable seed.

How it works

The studio configures Stable Diffusion 1.5 components with personalized weights. A CLIP text encoder conditions iterative U-Net denoising; a DDIM scheduler updates the latent, and a VAE decodes it into a 512 × 512 image. The default is 24 inference steps at guidance scale 7.5.

What is documented

The app describes DreamBooth personalization, but the published model repository does not include the original training run. Photo count, learning rate, training steps, and hardware are unverified. The studio distinguishes the general training method from the inference code that can be inspected.

What I would improve next

Create a repeatable gallery using fixed prompts and seeds, and evaluate likeness, prompt adherence, and visible artifacts. Record future training runs so the effect of each change can be compared. There is no independent quality benchmark for this checkpoint yet.

03

Software engineering
Reactive systems

Flicklytics

Making movie data useful, beyond a search result.

A five-person university project combining movie search with financial, review, and readability analysis. Built with Java, Play Framework, and asynchronous actors.

My work: the Financial Performance module, its Pekko actor and recovery strategy, and most of the HTML/CSS frontend.

  • Java
  • Play Framework
  • Pekko
  • TMDb API
Explore the source ↗Team project · local setup available
My contribution & engineering decisions

The problem

Movie information comes from an external API. The application needs to turn that data into useful analytics while handling delayed or failed requests.

My contribution

I designed a dedicated Pekko actor for asynchronous budget, revenue, and ROI calculations, added supervisor-based recovery for API failures, and built most of the frontend for search results and analytics views.

Team implementation

The wider application includes WebSocket search, review sentiment classification, readability scoring, and person statistics. It uses Guice dependency injection, with JUnit and Mockito tests. These are team capabilities; the public repository preserves source attribution.

Limitations & next steps

Results depend on the completeness of TMDb data; review sentiment is a heuristic output. The repository provides local setup instructions, but does not claim a live deployment. A useful next step would be documenting response times and recovery behavior under controlled API failures.

04

Full-stack development
Social applications

OurSpace

A personal space to talk, share, and stay connected.

A social application with a public interactive demo and a separate private experience. Visitors can explore messaging interactions without accessing real conversations.

My work: independently building the application’s interface and architecture, with AI-assisted development.

  • React
  • Vite
  • Firebase
  • Firestore
Try the demo ↗Source code
The experience, architecture & boundaries

The experience

The public demo uses fictional profiles. Visitors can send messages, reply, react, search, attach a local image, and edit a shared note. Demo state resets on refresh, and messages are not delivered to another visitor.

Architecture

The public demo runs on local in-memory state without Firebase imports. A separate private route loads the Firebase-backed application for approved accounts, with authentication, database, and storage access rules.

What I would improve next

The separation makes the product easier to demonstrate without exposing personal content. The private prototype still needs deeper review of shared-content ownership, schema validation, and media access before being treated as a production messaging service.

A little about me

I like seeing an idea become something I can use, question, and improve.

My work moves between machine learning and the software around it: preparing data, testing models, building interfaces, and connecting the pieces into an application.

I studied Computer Science with a focus on AI & ML at Sathyabama in Chennai. I’m now in Montréal, pursuing a master’s in Software Engineering at Concordia. Alongside language models and web development, I enjoy exploring the creative side of AI through personalized images.

What I want these projects to show is how I approach a problem, what I contributed, and where I still have more to learn.
